claims.text: High-temperature degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is driven by preferential oxidation of Cr and Ti at grain boundaries.
Oxidizing environments produce discontinuous, non-protective oxide patches in the alloy.
The discontinuous oxide patches spall and compromise microstructural integrity.
Reducing conditions limit surface oxidation while promoting internal oxidation.
Exposure under reducing conditions alters elemental diffusion and precipitate formation without producing a continuous surface scale.
The as-manufactured alloy is a homogeneous fcc material.
Al, Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Ti are uniformly distributed in the as-manufactured alloy.
Samples will be compared after exposure at approximately 800 °C in air and in an H2/Ar atmosphere.
Exposure durations will range from 50 to 200 hours.
Cr- and Ti-oxide-enriched grain boundaries act as weak spots for spallation or microstructural destabilization.
Altered reactive-element diffusion under reducing conditions promotes internal oxidation and precipitate formation.
Internal oxidation and precipitate formation under reducing conditions may weaken the fcc matrix.
Air exposure will yield Cr- and Ti-enriched oxides at grain boundaries, oxide spallation, and reduced mechanical performance.
H2/Ar exposure will yield internal oxidation and elemental redistribution without a continuous surface scale.
The as-manufactured alloy has an intact phase distribution and excellent strength and fatigue performance.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply near 800 °C during 50–200 hours of exposure in air or reducing H2/Ar.
Different temperatures, durations, or gas regimes may produce different oxidation or degradation behavior.
